problem_heading: Detention cases are won by families who move in the first week

problem_cards.title: Transfers scatter people fast
problem_cards.body: Detainees are routinely moved — often within days — to facilities hundreds of miles away, in different court jurisdictions, harder to visit and harder to defend. Getting a lawyer on record (Form G-28) and a bond request moving before a transfer is the single most time-sensitive move a family can make.

problem_cards.title: Bond is won with a package, not a plea
problem_cards.body: The judge weighs family ties, a stable address, work history, community roots, any record, and whether a sponsor will take responsibility. Families who show up with sponsor letters, proof of address, and documents win bonds; families who show up with only love and worry usually don't. We build that package with you in days.

problem_cards.title: The most damage happens with a signature
problem_cards.body: Detained people are handed papers — stipulated removal orders, voluntary departure agreements — that can waive the right to ever see a judge. Signing to "get out faster" can mean leaving faster, permanently. The message to get to your loved one today: sign nothing, and say you want to speak with a lawyer.

why_points.title: Built for the family on the outside
why_points.body: You're the one who can act. We work through you: you hire us, we get on record with the facility and the court, and we keep you informed at every step — in English or Spanish.

why_points.title: Location to release, one team

why_points.title: Straight answers under pressure
why_points.body: Some detention is mandatory by law, and no honest lawyer pretends otherwise. We tell you within the first review whether bond is realistic, what it will take, and what the alternatives are.

why_points.title: Flat fees, stage by stage
why_points.body: The bond stage is quoted as one flat fee before we start. The defense case that follows is quoted separately — so a family in crisis is never signing a blank check.

process.title: Locate and get on record
process.body: With a name, country of birth, and ideally the A-number, we find the facility, file the G-28 attorney appearance, and make contact — usually within a business day.

process.title: Bond strategy
process.body: We analyze eligibility (including whether any record triggers mandatory detention), identify the sponsor, and assemble the release package: letters, address proof, ties, employment.

process.title: The bond hearing
process.body: We request the earliest possible hearing, present the package, prepare the sponsor and your loved one to answer the judge, and argue for the lowest realistic bond.

process.title: After release: the real case
process.body: Release is the beginning, not the end — the removal case continues in court. We screen every form of relief and keep defending, with your family member home while we fight.

fees_heading: What does a detention case cost?
fees_body: The bond stage — locating, entering appearance, building the package, and the hearing — is one flat fee, quoted on the first call. The removal defense that continues after release is quoted separately by stage. The bond itself is set by the judge (the legal minimum is $1,500; grants commonly run higher) and is refunded at the end of the case when your loved one attends every hearing. We itemize all of it so a family in crisis can plan.

faq.q: How do I find someone detained by ICE?
faq.a: Use ICE's Online Detainee Locator (locator.ice.gov): search by A-number and country of birth, or by name, date of birth, and country. The A-number — a 9-digit number on any immigration paperwork — is the key that unlocks everything, so look for old documents. People booked in the last day or two may not appear yet, and detainees are moved between facilities without notice. If you can't find them, that's exactly the first thing we do.

faq.q: Can my loved one get out on bond?
faq.a: Many detainees can — an immigration judge weighs family ties, a stable address, work history, community roots, and any record, and a strong sponsor package moves every one of those factors. But certain criminal history triggers mandatory detention with no bond, and people stopped at entry face a different process (parole). We analyze which category applies in the first review and tell you straight.

faq.q: How much is immigration bond, and how is it paid?
faq.a: The legal minimum is $1,500; judges commonly set bonds in the several-thousand to tens-of-thousands range depending on the case. It's paid in full at an ICE bond office — and here's the detail families must plan for: the person who pays must show they're lawfully present in the U.S. If you don't have status yourself, line up a relative or friend who does. The money is refunded at the end of the case as long as your loved one attends every hearing.

faq.q: How fast can a bond hearing happen?
faq.a: A bond request can be made at the first hearing or by written motion, and courts often schedule bond hearings within days to a few weeks — the wait varies by court and season. What the family controls is readiness: the sponsor, the address proof, and the letters. When the package is ready the moment the court is, no time is wasted. That's why we start building it on day one.

faq.q: Should they sign anything ICE gives them?
faq.a: Not before a lawyer reads it. Stipulated removal orders and voluntary departure papers can waive the right to see a judge at all — people sign thinking it speeds up release and instead it speeds up removal. Everyone in detention has the right to say two things: "I do not want to sign" and "I want to speak with a lawyer." Get that message to your loved one through the facility phone as soon as you can.

faq.q: I don't have papers myself. Is it safe for me to hire a lawyer or visit?
faq.a: Hiring a lawyer is safe — we work for your family member, not the government, and what you tell us in seeking legal help is confidential. Two practical cautions: the person who pays the bond must have lawful status (plan who that will be), and visiting a facility generally requires ID, so many families send a documented relative or friend to visit while staying fully involved through us.
